definition: The Automated Mathematician (AM) is one of the earliest successful discovery systems.
details: It was created by Douglas Lenat in Lisp, and in 1977 led to Lenat being awarded the IJCAI Computers and Thought Award. AM worked by generating and modifying short Lisp programs which were then interpreted as defining various mathematical concepts; for example, a program that tested equality between the length of two lists was considered to represent the concept of numerical equality, while a program that produced a list whose length was the product of the lengths of two other lists was interpreted as representing the concept of multiplication. The system had elaborate heuristics for choosing which programs to extend and modify, based on the experiences of working mathematicians in solving mathematical problems.

explainer.lead: The Automated Mathematician, or AM, was an early computer system for discovering mathematical concepts rather than merely calculating with concepts supplied in advance. Created by Douglas Lenat in Lisp, it showed how heuristic rules could guide a program to generate and modify its own mathematical ideas.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a machine that invents little recipes and then tries to work out what mathematical idea each recipe represents. AM could turn a recipe about list lengths into ideas such as “these numbers are equal” or “multiply these numbers.” It used rules of thumb, inspired by working mathematicians, to decide which recipes were worth changing next.
tiers.practitioner: AM is best understood as a historical Lisp-based discovery system: its search space consists of short programs, and its operators extend or modify those programs. Heuristics prioritize the next program to change, while the resulting behavior must then be interpreted as a mathematical concept. A key pitfall is treating that interpretation as unrestricted mathematical understanding; the examples rely on specific operations over list lengths.
tiers.paperLevel: AM searches a space of short Lisp programs by heuristic extension and modification, then interprets program behavior as mathematical concepts. For example, |a| = |b| represents numerical equality, while constructing a list of length |a| × |b| represents multiplication. Its concept representations and search choices are therefore tied to executable Lisp behavior and mathematician-inspired heuristics.

explainer.example: A program that tests whether two lists have equal lengths, |a| = |b|, is interpreted as numerical equality. Another program constructs a list whose length is |a| × |b|, so AM interprets its behavior as multiplication.

usedIn.name: Automated discovery research
usedIn.detail: AM is an early successful example of a system designed to discover concepts through heuristic search.

usedIn.name: Mathematical concept exploration
usedIn.detail: Its short programs were interpreted as representations of ideas including numerical equality and multiplication.

explainer.intuition: Instead of writing down every mathematical concept beforehand, let the computer create small procedures and recognize concepts in what those procedures do. Rules of thumb guide which procedures to change, much as experience guides a mathematician toward promising lines of exploration.
howItWorks: Start with short Lisp programs whose behavior can describe mathematical ideas.
Use elaborate heuristics, based on mathematicians’ problem-solving experience, to choose promising programs.
Extend or modify the selected programs to generate new candidates.
Interpret each candidate’s behavior as a possible mathematical concept.
explainer.whyItMatters: AM was one of the earliest successful discovery systems, demonstrating that heuristic program modification could be used to explore mathematical concepts. Its creation also led to Douglas Lenat receiving the IJCAI Computers and Thought Award in 1977.
misconceptions: AM generated and modified programs; it did not simply retrieve concepts from a fixed catalogue.
A program represented a concept through interpretation of its behavior, as in the list-length construction for multiplication.
The 1977 IJCAI Computers and Thought Award was awarded to Douglas Lenat.
